data.title: Asiaâs central banks are discovering what interest rates cannot fix
data.description:
ASIA entered 2026 on a relatively strong footing. Then the war in the Middle East and disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz delivered an energy shock that hit the region particularly hard, causing inflation to climb again.

But no rate increase can reopen a shipping lane or lower the price of fertiliser. The harder question for central banks in Asia is what monetary policy can still do, and what must be left to others.

The region is living with two forces at once. The boom in semiconductors and artificial-intelligence infrastructure explains much of Asia’s resilience, from Taiwan and South Korea to Singapore, Malaysia and Vietnam.

But the gains are concentrated, and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) expects energy-importing economies outside this technology chain to face the hardest outlook.

Even where the AI boom is strong, central banks are left with one policy rate for two economies: a booming export sector and households squeezed by energy costs.

Nvidia is also increasingly investing in, lending to or guaranteeing the companies that buy its chips. It rejects the charge of circular financing, but such arrangements are a potential risk.

If evidence grew that vendor finance, rather than final demand, was supporting chip orders and prices, a repricing would hit Asia’s chipmakers first.

One shock, different constraints

For energy importers such as the Philippines and India, the risk is that higher fuel and food prices feed into wages and expectations. Both have raised rates, accepting slower growth to keep inflation from becoming entrenched.

Indonesia faces the hardest choice. With foreign investors selling Indonesian assets and the rupiah near its record low, Bank Indonesia surprised markets on Nov 18 by raising rates to 6 per cent, its first increase since June.

It paired the move with hedging incentives and the use of its reserves. Higher rates support the currency, but they weigh on growth.

It is a familiar predicament. The Asian financial crisis showed that intervention can buy time, but it cannot substitute for credibility once investors begin to doubt policy.

Indonesia’s buffers today are far stronger than in 1997. By moving pre-emptively, ahead of possible US Federal Reserve rate rises and rather than waiting for the rupiah to fall further, Bank Indonesia appears to have taken that lesson to heart.

Yet even central banks that have tightened cannot produce more oil. As the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has argued, with supply-driven inflation, the task is to prevent second-round effects. Yet with retail inflation now above RBI’s tolerance band, it may be falling behind the curve. Overdo it, and a central bank adds a growth shock to an energy shock.

Fiscal choices also shape what central banks face. Singapore and the Philippines largely let higher fuel prices pass through, while India, Indonesia and Malaysia absorbed much of the shock through subsidies.

These hold down headline inflation for now, but the bill lands on budgets just as borrowing costs rise. From my time in India’s Fifteenth Finance Commission, I know how hard such subsidies are to unwind. Targeted support for poorer households is the better route.

How far should a central bank go?

Under these circumstances, the region is figuring out what the remit of a central bank really is.

In Thailand, governor Vitai Ratanakorn has focused on problems that rates alone cannot solve, from high household debt to weak productivity. These are not problems central banks usually take on; their main tools are interest rates and bank supervision.

“If the economy is doing badly, people are getting poorer and businesses are closing, you can’t say that has nothing to do with us,” he has said.

The Bank of Thailand has cut rates – and also launched debt-relief initiatives. There is a logic to that. A rate cut does little for a household that cannot restructure its debts.

But debt restructuring and credit allocation also involve fiscal costs and choices about who gains and who loses. Those normally belong to elected governments, not central banks.

A central bank can justify stepping in where broken financial plumbing blocks monetary transmission, but it needs a clear exit and someone to answer to.

Mandates across the region also differ. The Monetary Authority of Singapore combines monetary policy with financial supervision, while Indonesia and South Korea separate much of supervision from central banking.

As more financial risk moves into funds and leveraged intermediaries beyond central banks’ reach, countries should not rush to widen bankers’ mandates. Better information-sharing between agencies matters more.

China’s prices, the region’s problem

While domestic policies matter, the influence of larger economies cannot be overstated.

China’s weak household demand is well known. What matters more for Asia is what China’s prices send abroad.

For about three years, falling Chinese factory prices exported disinflation, holding down goods inflation across the region and giving central banks room to ease, while squeezing manufacturers in Thailand, Indonesia and elsewhere.

But the Middle East energy shock has pushed China’s producer prices to their fastest rise in more than four years, thinning that cushion just when central banks need it.

This may not last. With domestic capacity large and demand weak, China’s producer prices are expected to fall again once energy prices ease, bringing back both the cushion and the competitive pressure to Asia.

Neither swing justifies sharp moves in rates; both argue for close attention to exchange rates and wages.

Japan matters to the global financial system through a different channel. As the Bank of Japan raises rates gradually, Japanese investors with large foreign portfolios may draw money out of Asian and US bond markets.

That, in turn, could push up yields globally. As governor Kazuo Ueda noted in his Michel Camdessus Lecture at the IMF on Nov 6, Japan’s persistent current-account surplus reflects investment income and corporate caution, not just trade.

Independence under pressure

Washington still sets much of the context within which Asia’s central banks operate. The Fed’s return to rate rises in September and large US deficits keep upwards pressure on global yields.

Hence, even when local conditions call for easier policy, central banks may be forced to raise rates to stop capital leaving, as Bank Indonesia did on Nov 18.

High public debt in most parts of the world adds a quieter danger. Governments facing higher borrowing costs may press central banks to keep rates low or prop up bond markets.

That is how fiscal dominance creeps in. Supporting market liquidity is a legitimate central-bank task; the test is whether it keeps markets working – or keeps sovereign deficits financed. No law alone protects central bank independence if fiscal policy is not credible.

Central banks still face the fundamental task of stopping supply shocks from turning into persistent inflation. But the harder work lies with governments: replacing broad subsidies with targeted help, spending and auditing public money better, and investing in energy security and skills.

For Asean, the regional safety net has just been finally strengthened: On Nov 11, an amended Chiang Mai Initiative Multilateralism (CMIM) Agreement added a Rapid Financing Facility to its US$240 billion swap pool, giving members quicker access to support after sudden shocks.

But the CMIM has never actually been drawn on. It remains to be seen whether members are willing to use it when it is needed.

In 1997, I was at the IMF and, as the Thailand financial crisis erupted, began working on its stabilisation programme. The lesson I took from then was that markets eventually test whatever policymakers leave undone.

Asia is far stronger today. But the same test is coming, and the main tool central banks have – adjusting interest rates – will not be enough to pass it.

The writer is a distinguished fellow at the Centre for Social and Economic Progress and Niti Aayog, the government of India’s policy think tank. He was formerly Asia-Pacific director at the IMF, adjunct professor at Georgetown University and managing director at JPMorgan.  

This essay is part of New Global Order, which explores how the changing world landscape is reshaping business, politics and beyond.

data.title: Tech companies growing their business in Apac see Singapore as a useful base
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] For customer relationship management software platform Klaviyo, artificial intelligence supercharges the business’ potential.

“There’s the data that we have on customer interactions, what can we do with that data, AI all of a sudden lets us do way more,” Ed Hallen, the co-founder and chief strategy officer at Klaviyo, told The Business Times.

The US-based company’s platform lets companies reach out to customers via different communication channels from e-mail to text to WhatsApp and phone calls.

With AI, brands can glean insights into individual customers, such as preferences for contact to be via text or call, and even what actions have led to customer service recovery.

“We found that AI is like a perfect sidekick for the marketer who can all of a sudden do way more than they ever could before,” said Hallen.

Currently, Klaviyo has more than 150 employees in Asia-Pacific (Apac), of which about 25 are based in Singapore.

These efforts have paid off for Klayivo, which reported a 25 per cent increase in third-quarter 2026 revenue to US$387.2 million from US$310.8 million in Q3 2025. The company, which is listed on the New York Stock Exchange, also reported a net income of US$704,000, recovering from a loss of US$426,000.

But AI will not replace humans entirely; instead, it can support marketing staff or interact with customers in some situations, said Hallen. For example, this could be handling a return on a product or recommendation where the process can be handled by AI.

While AI can help grow the business, being closer to customers is another advantage.

To better grasp the opportunities in the region, Klaviyo opened its Apac headquarters in Singapore in August 2026. Previously, the company concentrated on growing its presence in Australia, but soon realised that Singapore would be geographically closer to the customers they were seeing growth from.

In Apac, Klaviyo wants to help brands exercise more control over their relationships with customers. This is because with e-commerce, marketplaces such as Shopee and Lazada are the ones building a closer relationship with customers.

So, the question is how to control more of that relationship with the marketplace “or build that direct one-to-one relationship with the consumer is the same top of mind”, said Hallen.

In Apac, the issue facing brands is about cross-border customer relationships and how to manage them. Each market has different regulations around data management and consent, as well as different languages to navigate.

Coming to Singapore also allows for the company to tap the talent base here, said Hallen.

“We want people to work with our customers who understand marketing, who understand AI, who are really able to think cross-border and across the region entirely; Singapore is a great fit,” he added.

AI for lawyers

Another company finding success in Singapore is Legora, a legal AI platform that helps lawyers and legal departments with tasks such as research, drafting and review.

The entry into Apac “has been meteoric” said CEO Max Junestrand who co-founded Legora in Stockholm. The company opened its Singapore office in May 2026.

“The team in Singapore will be almost 20 by the end of the year and across Apac, we are over 100,” said Junestrand.

By being early adopters of AI, law firms and in-house legal departments have helped Legora, he noted. Apac is a competitive market for the legal sector and that has led to a higher adoption rate for AI.

Users in the region have gone beyond just using AI as an assistant in their legal work and using it from research to drafting and reviewing documents, something that Junestrand reckons offers exciting opportunities.

“I think the reception of our team... here on the ground as well has been extremely positive, and it sends us the signals to continue investing even more, and that there’s a lot of expansion opportunity,” he added.

Other than serving lawyers, Legora is also working with educational institutions such as the National University of Singapore in developing programmes to train lawyers-to-be in using AI for legal work.

“So that they can learn when to use AI, when to think critically,” said Junestrand.

Legora is not the only AI platform for the legal sector operating in Singapore, as US-headquartered Harvey has also made efforts here. Harvey appointed Stewart Garrett as head of Apac in October 2026. He is based in Singapore.

For Junestrand, the competition does not matter much to Legora, with his focus on building up the team, product and serving customers.

data.title: Stocks to watch: Keppel Infrastructure Trust,  Elite UK Reit, Thakral, Katrina
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Nov 20):

Keppel Infrastructure Trust (KIT) : KIT secured S$200 million in revolving loan facilities, with outstanding loans immediately repayable if its trustee-manager ceases to be wholly owned by Keppel Capital and/or Keppel, or ceases to act as KIT’s trustee-manager and a replacement wholly owned by the Keppel companies is appointed beforehand. Neither trigger had occurred yet, but if either leads to cross defaults, about S$1.9 billion in total facilities could be affected. The counter ended 1 per cent or S$0.005 higher at S$0.50 on Thursday, before the news.

Elite UK Reit : The manager of the real estate investment trust (Reit) submitted a planning application for a 352-bed student accommodation development in Wales. It expects a decision in 2027 and aims to start demolition and construction in 2028, subject to approval. The counter ended 1.7 per cent or £0.005 lower at £0.295 on Thursday, before the news.

Thakral : Thakral is selling its remaining 6.1 per cent stake in The Beauty Tech Group (TBTG), netting S$56.5 million, and expects to record a S$17.9 million gain over its end-June book value of S$38.6 million. Including the partial sale at TBTG’s initial public offering last year, the investment returned about S$70 million in cash to Thakral. The group plans to use the latest proceeds for new investments, its existing businesses and other capital needs. Shares of Thakral ended flat at S$1.45 on Thursday, before the announcement.

Katrina Group : An entity linked to carmaker BYD raised its stake in the F&B operator to 13.09 per cent from 4.91 per cent after buying more than 21 million shares for S$500,000 in an off-market transaction. It became a substantial shareholder in September, when it acquired a 5 per cent stake by buying 12.6 million shares from Katrina’s CEO for S$299,880. Shares of Katrina ended 8.3 per cent or S$0.003 higher at S$0.039 on Thursday, before the news.

data.title: Alice Huangâs links to the chip underworld
data.description:
THE Chinese businesswoman romantically linked to former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang had connections to a network for supplying AI chips that included an alleged Cambodian criminal enterprise, an FT investigation has found.

Former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang is at the centre of US investigations into whether Nvidia’s largest client in South-east Asia was involved in the underground chip trade. Some US officials suspect Alice Huang was a Chinese spy, a claim Beijing has dismissed as a “smear”.

Linked to Alice Huang was a sprawling web of companies between Nvidia and China-based users of its chips that included cloud computing partners, online gaming tycoons, Cambodian traffickers and hundreds of shell companies, the FT found.

These seemingly unconnected enterprises combined — without necessarily being aware of the full picture — to make billions of dollars from one of the most profitable illicit trades in the world: moving Nvidia chips into China.

The FT traced the connections after speaking to more than a dozen people with knowledge of the operations, revealing links that were obscured by complex structures through hundreds of corporate filings.

Nvidia’s advanced chips are crucial in developing cutting-edge AI and have become a vital commodity in the geopolitical rivalry between the US and China.

Washington’s export controls to prevent Beijing from acquiring the most powerful processors have created a multibillion-dollar black market to circumvent US curbs and satisfy China’s insatiable demand.

“Chip smuggling isn’t different from drugs or arms in terms of the structure of the supply chain. But there’s this importance attached to the semiconductor industry — it’s how the US wants to delay China in the AI race,” said Chris Clague, an associate fellow at International Institute for Strategic Studies who has focused on illicit trades in the past decade.

Moving advanced chips into China requires three main corporate channels: a group that is permitted to acquire and distribute the semiconductors; customers that do not fall foul of US export restrictions; and an underground network to smuggle the goods into China and money out.

The network linked to Alice Huang reached the US through Inspur, which was one of Nvidia’s largest partners for assembling chips into ready-to-use servers in China.

In March of 2023, Inspur was added to the US “entity list” for allegedly assisting the Chinese military. Some of its affiliates were also added to the register — but not Inspur’s part-owned US subsidiary, based in San Jose, California.

Inspur renamed the US unit Aivres, and since it was not on the entity list, it was able to keep trading with Nvidia.

Inside the chipmaker, there were questions about whether Aivres should qualify as an original equipment manufacturing (OEM) partner because of its links to Inspur, according to a person with direct knowledge of the matter. But Nvidia concluded the company met all compliance and export control requirements.

The second plank of the network was a customer that met the requirements to buy Nvidia chips at scale. OEM partners such as Aivres, which are allowed to integrate Nvidia GPUs into systems and sell those on, still needed to prove that their customers are not Chinese to access the US chipmaker’s products.

To be a qualified end customer, Nvidia requires at least three years of corporate records and proof that its management and owners are not majority Chinese.

Seeking to regain access to chip supplies, some of Inspur’s Chinese clients sought help from a successful online gaming company, Century Huatong, according to multiple people with knowledge of the matter.

Over two decades, the Chinese group had morphed from a car parts business into a gaming platform, finally emerging as a data centre investor with deep connections in the industry.

Century Huatong veterans discussed ways to gain access to the chips with its associates and business partners. The solution that emerged involved using an offshore shell company that would not trigger US export restrictions and could be branded as a “neocloud” provider.

That shell became Megaspeed, while Alice Huang fulfilled the requirement for a “trusted” outward-facing executive with a spotless record, according to people with knowledge of the arrangement.

Huang’s husband, Kang Wei, was an early investor in Century Huatong, according to Chinese corporate filings. His fund Hexi Investment also backed a 2020 Century Huatong data centre project with 7Road, a Shenzhen-based gaming company in which both Huang and Century Huatong had invested.

Alice Huang and Kang Wei did not respond to requests for comment.

7Road International, the offshore arm of 7Road, was the forerunner of Megaspeed, having had several years of clean corporate records in Singapore. In 2023, Huang acquired its unit in the city-state and renamed it.

An Nvidia spokesperson said: “We placed Megaspeed and a subsidiary on our block list in 2025 . . . we do not sell to them, and if one of our OEM customers identifies the company for any planned shipment, we do not approve the OEM sale.” Nvidia added that it had also restricted sales to Aivres.

Megaspeed did not respond to a request for comment but has previously said that it “conducts legitimate and lawful business”.

With her English skills, Hong Kong residency and reputation as a good networker and dealmaker, Huang was seen as an ideal western-friendly representative, according to people who knew her at the time.

It also helped that she and her husband were already looking to move into data centre businesses in south-east Asia that would lease chips to Chinese tech companies.

“Alice was chosen [to lead Megaspeed] because of the trust built over years,” said a person who had business dealings with her around the time.

The third — and essential — element of the enterprise was finding a partner to move chips into China.

People familiar with the matter said that Hu Xiaowei, who US authorities say is a leading figure in a Cambodia-based syndicate sanctioned for cyber scams and money laundering, filled at least part of this role.

Hu, who was arrested in Japan in the summer, could not be reached for comment. He has been accused by US authorities of running smuggling and gambling rings as the “second-in-command” at Prince Group.

A spokesperson for the Prince group of companies said Hu has never worked for the business and there was “no evidence of the US government’s unsupported allegations”.

Hu made money from online gaming-related businesses that brought him into contact with Century Huatong, according to people with knowledge of the matter.

The connections between Hu and Century Huatong run through a complex web of shareholdings and an IP partnership spanning dozens of company records examined by the FT.

One clear link can be traced through Wang Ji, Century Huatong’s chair and largest individual shareholder, who was the majority owner of a now-dissolved Ningxia-based company where Hu served as a director.

Another director of the dissolved company owns a Chongqing-based firm that controls multiple gaming entities associated with Fang Zhizhen, whom the US has sanctioned for allegedly laundering money for Prince Group.

Prince Group’s spokesperson said there was no evidence of a connection between Fang and the group.

Century Huatong’s ties to the alleged Prince Group leadership date back to about 2015, when the gaming platform began a process to ultimately acquire Shanda Games, owner of the Chinese rights to the viral game Legend of Mir in a landmark US$4.2 billion transaction.

Hu and his associates were involved in a group that hosted the Legend of Mir games on private servers, a hugely profitable business. Several members were arrested in 2016 for IP infringement, a case recently overturned due to corruption within the investigation, according to state media reports.

Around the time of the arrests, Hu moved to Cambodia, according to two people from the online gaming industry who knew him.

Online games are commonly used for money laundering because virtual currencies or in-game items can be bought with illicit funds and then sold on the secondary market to make the money appear legitimate.

The games groups have also long been in Nvidia’s orbit: before the chipmaker shifted focus to power the AI industry in 2022, the biggest demand for its GPUs in China was for gaming and crypto.

“If you look at the people and entities involved in today’s chip smuggling, lots of familiar names are from online gaming back in the day,” said a person who was involved in gaming deals.

“Many of them developed ‘grey’ side businesses such as money laundering and already built the infrastructure onshore and offshore to move money and goods around,” the person added.

Prince Group’s alleged “grey” infrastructure, some of the most extensive in the region, ranged from elaborate shell company structures to underground financing channels via online games and crypto, according to the people familiar with its operations.

The Prince Group spokesperson said it did not “have an illicit network” and there was “no foundation for claiming the existence of one, other than the unsupported US allegations in an indictment already proven to be riddled with falsehoods and temporal impossibilities”.

The group is also alleged to have physically smuggled goods via a fleet of private and business jets purchased by Hong Kong-based aircraft leasing companies that Hu founded, the people said. The Prince Group spokesperson said the allegation “has zero factual basis”.

By mid-2023, the elements were in place for the rise of Megaspeed. It officially approached Nvidia, pitching itself as a neocloud company with data centres in Malaysia and a leasing contract with Alibaba.

Led by Huang, Megaspeed passed the chipmaker’s compliance checks and quickly became one of its largest clients in the region.

Along the way, Alice Huang developed a close relationship with Nvidia’s chief Jensen Huang, according to multiple industry insiders. Her nickname in the Chinese data centre circles was “Jensen’s personal assistant”.

At Megaspeed, business was booming. The declared value of goods imported from Aivres by Speedmatrix, a Megaspeed subsidiary in Malaysia, was about US$4.6 billion between December 2024 and December 2025, according to ImportGenius trade data.

Many of those chips ended up in China, according to multiple people with knowledge of the matter.

A raid by Indonesian police in early 2026 found empty server racks with no GPUs at the local Megaspeed subsidiary, according to Singapore’s Straits Times.

Multiple people involved in chip distribution channels said that once the Nvidia products passed through smuggling routes in South-east Asia — a process that can involve multiple countries and take weeks — they moved to the black market in China, where they were sold at multiples of their original price.

Once the chips were inside China, one of the key distributors of the smuggled Nvidia chips in the country was Shanghai Century Litong, which was established by a subsidiary of Century Huatong, according to people with knowledge of the transactions. The Information first reported Century Litong’s role in the network of Nvidia chip trade in China.

Corporate filings suggest Alice Huang was again linked to the formation of the group. With her sister, Huang Yu, she controlled an investment vehicle that had a joint venture with Century Huatong called Shanghai Century Longteng.

Longteng later founded Century Litong. Bloomberg reported that restricted Nvidia chips were found in Longteng-related data centres in Shanghai.

The FT revealed last year that at least US$1 billion worth of smuggled Nvidia chips were sold in China in just three months after President Trump tightened controls on H20, a less powerful chip made for the Chinese market to meet export control requirements.

People with knowledge of the smuggling operations say the layers of corporations were set up to mask the flow of AI chips into China. They also provided a useful buffer between the smuggling entities and the end users — some of which are China’s biggest tech groups.

Tencent and Alibaba, two of China’s biggest tech companies, both have business ties with Century Huatong. Tencent, China’s largest social media, messaging and gaming platform, has a 10.1 per cent stake in the company.

Century Huatong, through its fully owned subsidiary, invested in T3 Travel, a car-hailing business that also counts both Tencent and Alibaba as investors. Alice Huang is on the board of T3.

The FT has found no evidence to suggest that Tencent or Alibaba were involved in the chip smuggling businesses. Tencent said: “We are minority investors in a variety of internet and video game companies. We have no connection to nor knowledge of the other activities alleged in the story.”

Alibaba did not respond to a request for comment.

Inspur, Aivres, Century Huatong, 7Road, Shanghai Century Litong and Shanghai Century Longteng also did not respond to requests for comment.

Two US administrations have tried to protect the country’s lead over China in AI by restricting access to Nvidia’s most advanced processors. This week, the Trump administration announced further limits on how Chinese companies can access the chips via South-east Asia.

But it was US export controls that opened up a lucrative opportunity for those willing to break the rules, said Hanna Dohmen, senior research analyst at Georgetown University’s Centre for Security and Emerging Technology.

“When there’s a significant demand not met, you get smuggling,” said Dohmen. “We need to be realistic about what export controls can achieve. It doesn’t mean no US chip will make its way to China. When you put a lid on South-east Asia, would they not just go to other countries?” THE FINANCIAL TIMES

data.title: HDB plans new seaside housing in Pasir Ris, proposes to retain 13 ha of greenery, coastal habitats
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The government is planning to provide new homes in the eastern suburb of Pasir Ris, a popular residential location, and has proposed retaining about 13 hectares (ha) of greenery and coastal habitats as it seeks to make room for homes while limiting the impact on ecologically important areas.

The site, to be called Pasir Ris Neighbourhood 3, sits at the eastern edge of Pasir Ris Town and is bounded by Pasir Ris Drive 3, Pasir Ris Drive 4, Jalan Loyang Besar and Sungei Loyang.

The area has been reserved for residential use since Master Plan 1980, “with this planning intention reaffirmed at each subsequent Master Plan review conducted every five years”, the Housing & Development Board said in a release on Monday (Nov 23).

Under the conceptual plan for the new neighbourhood, about 5 ha of terrestrial greenery and the full 8 ha of coastal habitats will be kept. Green buffers and a proposed 15 m-wide linear park along Sungei Loyang will also support biodiversity and provide recreational spaces for residents. 

The proposed development comes amid “strong interest” for housing in the area, HDB said. The last three Build-To-Order (BTO) projects in Pasir Ris – Costa Grove in 2020 and Costa Riviera I and II in 2024 – each recorded an application rate of 3.6 among first-timer families for four-room flats.

The most recent new launch in the Pasir Ris area – executive condominium (EC) project Coastal Cabana – sold 498 units, or more than 66 per cent of its total of 748 units, at an average price of S$1,734 per square foot at its launch in January 2026.

The government said it prioritises brownfield sites for housing and seeks to make better use of limited land, including by building taller and redeveloping sites with expired leases. 

However, no suitable alternative brownfield sites in and around Pasir Ris could provide a comparable amount of housing within the desired timeframe, HDB said.

It noted that the former Siglap Secondary School site is already being planned for future housing, while industrial sites at Lorong Halus, Pasir Ris West and Pasir Ris Coast Industrial Park 6 are needed for other national uses or cannot be made available in time. 

The new neighbourhood will house both public and private homes, amenities and community spaces, with plans taking into account an environmental impact assessment (EIA) and feedback from nature groups.

The assessment, conducted by Tembusu Asia Consulting, recorded 254 fauna species, 25 of which are of conservation significance, including the Sunda Pangolin. 

To protect the site’s habitats, the retained 5 ha terrestrial area would act as a buffer between the development, mangroves and an existing stream. It would also serve as a stepping-stone habitat for wildlife moving towards the sea and nearby islands, including Pulau Ubin. 

Separately, about 1 ha in the south-eastern corner of the 5 ha area may be needed for coastal protection measures, subject to further study. 

HDB is inviting public feedback on the EIA findings and conceptual plan from Nov 23 to Dec 20.

data.title: US tracked Alice Huangâs contacts with China spy agency during Nvidia affair
data.description:
[WASHINGTON] The Chinese woman at the heart of the Nvidia scandal kept in contact with an official of China’s top spy agency for more than a year while she was carrying out a secret affair with Jensen Huang, according to multiple people with knowledge of US intelligence reports that describe the encounters.

The woman, Alice Huang, was in touch with an officer of China’s Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 until the fall of this year, the people with knowledge of the intelligence said.

That period overlaps with at least a portion of the time she was in a relationship with Jensen Huang, then the head of the world’s leading maker of advanced artificial intelligence chips.

US intelligence agencies have also gathered evidence that Alice Huang’s business partner, Kang Wei, who was often introduced as her husband, worked with the same Chinese spy agency, the people said.

The extent and specific timing of Alice Huang’s contacts with the spy agency — and Kang’s work for the same intelligence service — have not been previously reported.

Alice Huang’s contacts with the Chinese spy agency last year and up through recent months help to flesh out how US officials came to believe that Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s CEO earlier this month, was the target of an intelligence operation.

They correspond not just to the time when he was conducting the affair but also to at least part of the period when Alice Huang’s company, Megaspeed, was acquiring large amounts of advanced Nvidia chips, some of which went to data centres in South-east Asia serving Chinese technology companies like Alibaba and some of which are suspected of being smuggled to China.

Allies of the former Nvidia chief, including President Donald Trump, have sought to minimise the scandal and questioned whether Alice Huang was spying for Chinese intelligence. But the newly revealed information underscores the continuous contacts that she had with the Ministry of State Security, even as she was in a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang.

It also helps to flesh out why some American officials have been worried that Alice Huang’s role is just one element of a much broader push by China in that technological battle. The Ministry of State Security has prioritised focusing on acquiring high-end chips and advancing China’s AI ambitions.

US officials are investigating the role of Alice Huang and Kang in a network of Southeast Asian companies, including Megaspeed, that have been linked to the possible smuggling of Nvidia chips to China, to evade US export control laws. US officials are still working to determine the full extent and duration of their work with Chinese intelligence.

The intelligence gathered by the US contains evidence — including shipping records — demonstrating the role of Alice Huang and Kang in that network of companies, people with knowledge of the intelligence reports said.

The New York Times has previously reported that Alice Huang and her family have a web of connections to Chinese defence contractors.

Jensen Huang initially described his relationship with Alice Huang as normal interactions with a business customer. He acknowledged an affair only after the Times revealed last month that Alice Huang had been identified by the United States as a Chinese intelligence asset and that the Nvidia chief had been picked up on electronic surveillance targeting her.

He stepped down this month after the Times subsequently reported that he had an affair with a subordinate at Nvidia. Administration officials never provided him with a so-called defensive briefing about Alice Huang, a heads-up that the woman he was in a relationship with had been linked to Chinese intelligence.

A spokesperson for Jensen Huang declined to comment. The White House, the State Department, the Chinese Embassy in Washington, Alice Huang and Kang did not respond to requests for comment on Sunday.

Before the scandal broke into public view, advisers to Trump told him on at least two occasions that US intelligence had uncovered Alice Huang’s links to the Chinese spy agency and that she was in a close relationship with Jensen Huang while he was still running Nvidia, according to US officials with direct knowledge of the briefings.

Both times, including when his national security adviser discussed it with him, the president downplayed the concerns and made clear he did not want to intervene in the matter.

The officials said Trump regarded Jensen Huang as a valuable ally and Nvidia as essential to the health of the American economy and stock market. Trump has recently suggested that Nvidia should consider bringing Jensen Huang back as CEO, a possibility the company’s board has rejected.

“We have to protect our brilliant people. Jensen is one of them,” the president said at a White House news conference on Friday. “I think the company if they were smart they’d take that brilliant man, accept an apology and let him go back to work.”

Trump has claimed that no one in his government told him of any intelligence indicating that Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset.

“I don’t know that she is a spy,” he said. “Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that’s a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she’s a spy.”

In fact, his administration has been monitoring Alice Huang’s contacts with the Chinese spy agency for more than a year, a period when the Ministry of State Security has been intensifying its new role in seeking to give China an advantage in artificial intelligence.

“This network of companies working to procure and smuggle Nvidia chips lines up precisely with the MSS’s recently stated core mission of circumventing and undermining US export controls on semiconductors and other key technologies,” said Matt Pottinger, who served as deputy national security adviser during Trump’s first term, and who is CEO of the open-source research firm Garnaut Global.

The Ministry of State Security has for decades declared that its mission is to combat espionage and to eliminate political threats to Communist Party rule in China. The minister of state security, Chen Yixin, gave a similar five-point statement as recently as late last year. Then in April, he unveiled a new, sixth mission — overcoming the “blockades” choking China’s access to key technologies like artificial intelligence. NYTIMES

data.title: DBS opens flagship investment strategy to retail investors with new fund
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Retail investors now have access to DBS’ flagship fund strategy through its new DBS Chief Investment Office (CIO) Barbell Strategy Fund.

The bank is making its strategy available – which was previously open to only wealth clients – to a wider group of investors through its fund, which has raised more than S$200 million during its two-week initial offer period.

Following the initial offer, the fund remains open for subscription via the DBS digibank app. Retail investors can make an initial investment of S$1,000, with regular savings plans available from S$100 a month.

Chua Yi Wen, Singapore head of investment products at DBS’ consumer banking group, said: “As market volatility becomes the new norm, we hope to enable our customers to invest consistently with greater confidence as they grow their wealth.”

Combining growth, income and alternatives in a single actively managed solution, the multi-asset fund is designed to help customers grow their wealth over time with active management through market cycles, said DBS.

The fund is guided by the DBS CIO Barbell Strategy, which delivered a cumulative net return of 72.8 per cent (7.9 per cent annualised) from its inception in 2019 to end-October 2026, outperforming the 45 per cent (5.4 per cent annualised) return of a reference index comprising equal weights of global equities and global bonds.

The fund seeks long-term capital growth through diversified exposure in multiple asset classes, combining three complementary return drivers: secular growth equities, diversified global fixed income, and alternatives such as gold and hedge funds.

This “barbell” portfolio construction allows investors to participate in long-term themes such as artificial intelligence, semiconductors, cloud computing and energy transition, while maintaining portfolio resilience through income-generating assets and diversifiers.

DBS Bank chief investment officer Hou Wey Fook said the strategy gives investors “exposure to long-term change alongside income and diversification to withstand setbacks”.

He added: “Its relevance today lies in helping investors remain committed to long-term structural opportunities that may take years to realise, even as markets focus on the next few months.”

DBS said the fund is managed by its discretionary portfolio management team, and is actively allocated and rebalanced in line with the CIO’s house view and changing market conditions, “freeing customers from the need to monitor, select and rebalance each underlying investment themselves”.

The new fund marks the latest in DBS’ efforts over the years towards lowering barriers to investing and widening access to wealth management solutions and expertise.

data.title: Stocks to watch: Yangzijiang Shipbuilding, Seatrium, Frencken
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 19):

Yangzijiang Shipbuilding : The shipbuilder’s subsidiary has entered into an investment agreement with China’s Taicang Port Economic and Technological Development Zone. The agreement is in relation to a project to develop a clean energy vessel intelligent manufacturing base in Taicang city, located in Jaingsu province. The group expects capital expenditure for the project to be about 3.38 billion yuan (US$507 million). Shares of Yangzijiang Shipbuilding ended 1.6 per cent or S$0.07 higher at S$4.39 on Wednesday, before the announcement.

Seatrium : The offshore, marine and energy specialist reported that its net order book stood at S$12.2 billion as at end-September, comprising 35 projects with deliveries extending through 2033. It had secured S$1.7 billion in new orders so far this year. Seatrium expects its underlying net profit for FY2026 to be materially higher than in FY2025. The counter ended 0.6 per cent or S$0.01 lower at S$1.71, before the news.

Frencken : The technology manufacturer announced on Wednesday (Nov 18) a 31.3 per cent year-on-year increase in earnings to S$13 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30. Revenue grew 12.8 per cent to S$238.5 million, from S$211.5 million a year earlier. The increase was mainly driven by Frencken’s mechatronics division’s revenue, which rose 13.4 per cent to S$214.3 million. The counter ended S$0.01, or 0.6 per cent, up at S$1.71 before the news.

data.title: Gold rebounds as traders pare bets on near-term Fed rate hikes
data.description:
GOLD rebounded from its biggest weekly decline in eight months as traders scaled back bets on the Federal Reserve raising interest rates in the near term. 

Bullion rose as much as 1.3 per cent to around US$3,582 an ounce, after falling 9 per cent last week to a 14-month low. Traders are paring expectations of monetary tightening after growing concerns about artificial intelligence spending rippled across markets, sending technology stocks plunging. 

Following the rout, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned the Fed risks jeopardising the US economy by overtightening in response to latest inflation data. His prior attempt to rein in elevated long-term borrowing costs sent yields lower in August, which sparked a brief rally in gold. 

Swaps traders are no longer fully pricing in a Fed rate hike in December after Treasury yields fell across the curve on Friday. The policy-sensitive two-year yields ended 12 basis points lower, a positive for non-yielding bullion. 

Gold has fallen by around a third since the US-Iran war erupted in late February as higher energy costs fuelled inflation, prompting central banks to raise rates. It’s traded below the US$4,000 support level since Nov 11.

Spot gold rose 1.1 per cent to US$3,578.24 an ounce at 8.26 am in Singapore, while silver was up 2.6 per cent at US$42.21 after tumbling 15 per cent the week before.

Platinum and palladium also advanced. The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index dipped 0.1 per cent after rising 0.6 per cent last week. BLOOMBERG
